Recall that sucrose is glucose plus fructose. Glucose is the 6-membered alpha pyranose ring and fructose is the 5-membered furanose ring.
walkthrough:
**Recall what sucrose is made from**

Sucrose is a disaccharide made by condensation of two different hexose monomers. It is glucose plus fructose, joined by a glycosidic bond with water removed.

So you are looking for: one glucose + one fructose.

**Tell glucose and fructose apart by ring size**

Glucose in solution forms a 6-membered pyranose ring with one $CH_2OH$ group. Fructose forms a 5-membered furanose ring with two $CH_2OH$ groups, one at each end of the ring.

Scan options A to D for ring size. Options A and B show two 6-membered rings, so they cannot be sucrose.

**Check the alpha glucose detail**

Only options C and D show a 6-membered plus 5-membered pair. Now look at carbon 1 of the glucose on the left, the carbon on the right side of the ring.

In option C the glucose has $H$ up and $OH$ down, which is alpha-glucose. That alpha-glucose plus fructose pair is exactly what forms sucrose.

options.A: Shows two 6-membered rings, so two aldohexoses, not glucose plus fructose. This cannot form sucrose.
options.B: Shows two identical 6-membered alpha-glucose rings. Glucose plus glucose forms maltose, not sucrose.
options.C: Shows a 6-membered alpha-glucose on the left plus a 5-membered fructose on the right. This is the correct glucose plus fructose pair for sucrose.
options.D: Shows a 5-membered fructose on the right but the 6-membered ring on the left is beta-glucose with OH up, not the alpha-glucose needed for sucrose.
